item.title: Alabama Power Announces $160 Million Rate Decrease for 2027 After Pushback on High Energy Costs
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Alabama Power announced Friday its electric rates would decrease across the board next year, saving its 1.5 million customers approximately $160 million on their energy bills.

The company attributed the savings to projected increases in revenue from large data center contracts next year.

“In January, our customers will see their rates go down because of the growth we’re seeing across the state,” Alabama Power CEO Jeff Peoples said in a news release. “Alabama is growing and we’re making sure that growth works for all of our customers.”

The company news release said that a home or business using 1,000 kilowatt-hours each month would save more than $50 a year, compared to current rates.

Electricity costs have been a major political issue in Alabama for the past year, after an Inside Climate News investigation last November showed Alabama Power customers paid the highest total electric bills in the country in 2024, driven by its above-average rates and Alabama’s very high electricity usage.

In filings made Friday with the Alabama Public Service Commission, the company announced a projected 2027 income of $1.76 billion, higher than its currently allowed rate of return set by the PSC.

Unlike most regulated utilities in the United States, Alabama Power operates under a formula-based rate mechanism called the Rate Stabilization and Equalization factor, created by the PSC in 1982.

Under that system, rates are adjusted up or down automatically every January based on the company’s projections for the upcoming year, without the formal rate case hearings that most other states use to set electricity rates.

Those projections for 2027 triggered the changes, which will take effect in January.

Alabama Power also said it will comply with the commission’s request to stop billing customers for part of its advertising budget beginning in 2027. That change is expected to save the average customer about four cents per month, the company said.

Critics Say Tax Cut, Not Data Centers, Drive Decrease

Daniel Tait, executive director of clean energy advocacy group Energy Alabama, said the company should not get credit for lowering rates when the formula dictated the decrease.

“Alabama Power customers should not be fooled,” Tait said in an email. “The utility wants a public parade for handing back money it was on track to overcharge customers.”

Donate Now

Tait also said the company is crediting data centers for the decrease, but does not mention that a massive cut in the company’s tax bill generated even more savings.

“The company credits data centers, but its own numbers show there would be no cut without a roughly $180 million drop in its tax bill, which the company ties to nuclear tax credits from the Inflation Reduction Act,” Tait said. “Even after this action, the company’s own filing shows its return on equity, a marker for its profits, remaining above the national average.”

Relief for Customers Paying Country’s Highest Bills

Two weeks after the ICN investigation was published last November, U.S. Sen. Katie Britt said Alabama had the “highest rates in the Southeast,” amid a debate about a hyperscale data center project currently under construction in Bessemer, just west of Birmingham.

In December, the PSC approved a two-year rate freeze proposed by Alabama Power, delaying scheduled increases surrounding the purchase of a gas-fired power plant, and blocking rate increases until 2028.

Then in the spring, fierce public backlash against high electricity prices spurred state lawmakers to pass sweeping utility legislation that will dramatically reshape the PSC, but will not require the formal rate case hearings that most other states use.

The bill will expand the PSC from three members to seven next year, and create a governor-appointed secretary of energy who will set the PSC’s agenda and “have authority over personnel and administrative functions of the commission.”

The secretary can only be overruled by a vote of five of the seven commissioners.

The two incumbent PSC commissioners on the ballot this year were defeated in GOP primaries, leaving PSC President Cynthia Lee Almond as the lone returning member next year.

Britt issued a news release Friday, taking credit for next year’s decrease.

“I asked Alabama Power to find a way to lower rates—not just freeze them, but achieve lower power bills for Alabama households,” Britt said in the release. “Today, I am excited to say that is happening.

“I am proud to have successfully led this charge and that it’s resulted in putting more money back in hardworking Alabamians’ pockets.”

Tait, from Energy Alabama, said the bigger issue is the high rate of return that Alabama Power earns. The company reported $1.52 billion in profit through the first three quarters of 2026.

“Alabamians want real relief on their electric bills, and that comes from a cut to what Alabama Power is allowed to profit,” he said. “Sure, people will take the $4 per month but shuffling tax credits around doesn’t cut it.”

item.title: Court Delays Plan to Detonate Toxic Explosives in Iowa
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Plans to detonate nearly 10,000 pounds of degraded lead azide at an Eastern Iowa ammunition plant are on hold after the Army postponed the operation and a federal appeals court temporarily halted an emergency permit from the Environmental Protection Agency.

Initially scheduled for Friday, the planned explosion generated immense public outcry and concern from public health experts, environmentalists and elected officials who say residents received inadequate notice and guidance regarding the impacts of lead dust on their health and the environment.

Lead azide is a common primary explosive in bombs. After decades in storage at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, 68 barrels of the compound have become dangerously unstable and require emergency disposal.

Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle announced late Thursday that the detonation would be rescheduled to Monday. But hours later, a ruling by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit placed an administrative stay on the EPA’s detonation permit, indefinitely delaying the operation.

The ruling came less than 24 hours after environmental law organization Earthjustice, representing the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club Iowa Chapter, sued the EPA over its permit and filed an emergency motion asking the court to suspend it.

In their suit, the petitioners argued that the decision-making process lacked transparency and that the Army failed to adequately explore alternatives to detonation. “Within the permit, we just do not see enough things that will protect human health and the environment,” said Thien Chau, a senior attorney for Earthjustice. He described the planned detonation as “abnormal and extraordinary.”

The court could rule on the emergency motion at any point in the next few days, Chau said.

A Ticking Time Bomb

During a March safety review at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, officials discovered that stored lead azide had dissolved and reformed into irregularly shaped, highly volatile crystals. Friction, heat or shock could easily trigger spontaneous detonation.

Rather than risk an accidental explosion by leaving the barrels in storage, relocating them or chemically neutralizing the contents, all alternatives the Army considered, the department opted to conduct a controlled detonation of nearly five tons of lead azide, according to its environmental assessment. The Environmental Protection Agency granted an emergency permit for the detonation last Friday, citing an “unacceptable” risk of accidental combustion.

Even with mitigation technology like blast containment barriers and water misters in place, the explosion will generate a lead-containing dust cloud that could deposit the neurotoxin across hundreds of miles in an area where tens of thousands of Iowans live.

Residents of Middletown were informed of the planned detonation at a town hall in October. But state officials and most Iowans learned about the explosion just days before it was scheduled to take place.

Maps released by the Army in a public advisory early this week projected surface deposition of lead 50 miles northwest of Middletown, with airborne exposure as far as 100 miles afield.

A spokesperson for Gov. Kim Reynolds said that the advisory was the first she had heard of the operation.

The projected ranges for the dust cloud shrank significantly in updated maps released Wednesday, which the Army says reflect changing weather forecasts. Their most recent projections showed toxic lead dust settling on surfaces over a smaller region that extends at least 30 miles north of the plant and up to 10 miles wide.

Planning for Toxic Debris

The Army’s projections suggest outdoor lead dust levels in the plume’s path could exceed federal benchmarks for indoor lead levels in homes and childcare facilities, said Patrick O’Shaughnessy, a professor of occupational and environmental health at the University of Iowa.

Still, the precise amount and location of lead that would be released by the blast is unknown and depends on weather conditions and the effectiveness of the Army’s engineered controls, O’Shaughnessy said.

According to the emergency permit issued by the Environmental Protection Agency, the Army is required to use high-end estimates to avoid underestimating the potential impact of the detonation. The Army did not respond to questions about more specific ranges of lead concentrations.

Leading up to the planned Friday detonation, the Army advised residents to stay indoors, close windows and doors, and set heating and cooling systems to “recirculate” for a few hours after the planned blast. The Army also advised residents to clean their cars and hose down play surfaces and windowsills once the cloud settled.

Any surfaces typically touched by children would be especially important to clean, said O’Shaughnessy. As a neurotoxin, lead is most harmful to small children and infants with developing brains and nervous systems.

The EPA emergency permit requires the Army to conduct monitoring before, during and after detonation. In addition, researchers at the University of Iowa scrambled to set up independent air and soil monitoring following the Army’s announcement early this week, said David Cwiertny, director of the university’s Center for Health Effects of Environmental Contamination.

This story is funded by readers like you.

Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.

Donate Now

Many residents of the heavily agricultural state have expressed concern about the lingering effects of lead dust for soil, crops and livestock, Cwiertny said. Scientists will rely on field samples taken after the explosion to gauge the impact on agriculture and animals.

“We know that unlike a porch or patio table, you cannot simply wipe down farm fields, gardens or topsoil, because those surfaces are hard to clean,” he said.

The Army has not issued specific guidance for livestock producers in the exposure zone. The Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship recommended livestock be kept at an alternate location or indoors until the air plume could pass.

The department also suggested that producers ask the U.S. Army to collect soil and forage samples at their farms after the detonation, power wash the exteriors of buildings and equipment and work with a veterinarian to monitor livestock for signs of lead poisoning.

Leaders Call For Clarity

On Thursday night, Gov. Reynolds issued a statement saying she had spoken to Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle and asked that he delay the detonation. Governor-elect Rob Sand and U.S. Senator-elect Josh Turek also called on military leadership to postpone the operation until Iowans could be given more information about the decision-making process.

In light of growing public interest in the detonation, the Department of the Army, Department of Health and Human Services and Environmental Protection Agency issued a joint statement Friday morning.

“Officials have been meticulously planning for this event since March, and all agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized,” the statement read.

item.title: US leases American Samoan seabed for mining in auction deemed illegal by court
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

- On Nov. 19, the U.S. government auctioned off 12.7 million hectares (31.5 million acres) of American Samoan seabed for $6 million, despite a federal court ruling that found the lease sale to be illegal for not taking into account impacts on endangered species.

- The lease sale marks the first time a country has completed an auction of seabed mineral leases that grant the right to explore for minerals.

- Critics warn that seabed mining in the waters of American Samoa could harm the marine environment and threaten the cultural, food security and economic interests of local communities.

- A pending legal challenge could invalidate the auction and any leases issued.

The U.S. government has auctioned off 12.7 million hectares (31.5 million acres) of the American Samoan seabed, despite public opposition and a federal court ruling that found the sale to be illegal. The sale marks the first time a country has completed an auction of seabed mineral leases that grant the right to explore for minerals.

The auction, which took place on the morning of Nov. 19 in Thousand Oaks, California, was publicly livestreamed, offering two vast lots of American Samoan seabed: One covering about 15 million acres, and the other about 16 million acres. Mongabay attended the livestream.

Just two bidders showed up: A U.S. company called Wetstone U.S. Ventures and the Norwegian company Adepth. However, only Wetstone participated in the bidding process. By the end of the auction, which lasted approximately 20 minutes, Wetstone had secured both leases at the starting price of $3 million each, equivalent to approximately 19 U.S. cents per acre.

In 2024, American Samoa, a U.S. territory, imposed a moratorium on deep-sea mining in waters extending up to 3 nautical miles from its coastline. The U.S. government has jurisdiction over the remainder of the exclusive economic zone (EEZ), which extends 200 nautical miles from shore, allowing it to pursue seabed mineral activities in this area without approval from the American Samoan government.

In a statement released on Nov. 16, a few days before the auction took place, Pulaali’i Nikolao Pula, the governor of American Samoa, called the lease sale an “historic moment” for his nation.

“For more than 3,000 years, our Polynesian ancestors explored and navigated the vast Pacific Ocean,” Pula said. “Today, we stand at the threshold of a new era of exploration, one that could unlock scientific knowledge, create economic opportunities, and strengthen American Samoa’s role in America’s strategic future in the Pacific.”

Critics say that any mining activities in this area would harm the marine environment, particularly the Rose Atoll Marine National Monument, a 34,964-square kilometer (13,500-square mile) protected reef ecosystem adjacent to the lease areas that supports a range of endangered and threatened species, including sea turtles, sharks and cetaceans. Members of the American Samoan community and their allies also argue that deep-sea mining would disregard the cultural, food security and economic importance of their waters.

The Marine Minerals Administration (MMA), a federal agency within the U.S. Department of the Interior (DOI), says it will responsibly pursue deep-sea mining in American Samoan waters, and that this activity is necessary to secure minerals critical for U.S. national security. Proponents of the industry argue that deep-sea minerals are needed for producing fighter jets, weaponry and renewable energy technologies.

The U.S. push to begin mining the deep sea follows U.S. President Donald Trump administration’s release in April 2025 of an executive order calling for the accelerated development of the industry. In addition to pursuing deep-sea mining in federal waters, the U.S. is also looking to mine in international waters, including in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone in the Pacific Ocean and the South Pacific Ocean.

Forty-five nations have called for a moratorium or precautionary pause on the industry due to a number of concerns, including the potential destruction of the marine environment and a lack of research on the impacts of the fledgling industry. Deep-sea mining has not yet begun on a commercial scale anywhere in the world.

Speaking just before the auction of the American Samoan seabed began, MMA Acting Director Michael Olsen said the lease sale was “another step in securing American self-reliance while honoring our responsibility to care for the waters and resources we’ll pass on to the next generation.”

“As we look to America’s next 250 years, we want future generations to inherit a nation that can build and innovate here at home, on the lands and in the waters that we’ve stewarded,” Olsen said.

Douglas Boren, who leads the MMA’s Pacific office, emphasized before the auction that the leases would only permit preliminary seabed surveys and data collection, and that any subsequent testing or commercial extraction would require further DOI approval and environmental review.

The lease sale proceeded despite a federal court in Hawaiʻi ruling on Nov. 16 in favor of community and conservation groups that had sued the National Marine Fisheries Service, an agency within the U.S. Department of Commerce’s National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, for violating the nation’s Endangered Species Act by greenlighting the deep-sea mining lease sale.

Chris Eaton, a senior attorney at the U.S. nonprofit environmental law organization Earthjustice, the group that represented the plaintiffs in the lawsuit, called the DOI’s decision to proceed with the lease sale “lawless.”

“I thought it was pretty remarkable that in the live auction, they didn’t even acknowledge that ruling,” Eaton told Mongabay. “They’re ignoring that a federal court said what they’re doing is illegal, and they’re proceeding as if everything is just fine.”

“I am not sure why they decided to go forward,” he added. “I think it was kind of a shock.”

Eaton said Earthjustice has a second motion pending against the MMA that challenges the agency’s legal authority to proceed with the sale. If successful, the motion could invalidate the auction process and any leases issued.

Sabrina Suluai-Mahuka, founder of Finafinau Foundation, an environmental organization in American Samoa that opposes deep-sea mining, said she was “filled with frustration.” On Nov. 19, Suluai-Mahuka and other environmental advocates took part in a protest outside the site of the auction in Thousand Oaks.

“It’s very mind-boggling to think that they can put a price tag on our home and our waters, as if the impacts are not going to be felt by the real people who live in the ocean,” Suluai-Mahuka told Mongabay. “But this also sets a blueprint for future lease sales like CNMI [Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands] and Guam and Alaska and Virginia.”

The next planned lease sale, for 27 million hectares (67 million acres) of seabed in the CNMI, is scheduled for Dec. 16.

“While we’re extremely disappointed, we’re actually not surprised with how aggressive this timeline has been in this process,” Suluai-Mahuka said. “But this is not the end of our fight. We are going to continue to fight with every single bit of our being to protect our home and our children’s futures.”

Banner image: A helmet jellyfish (Periphylla periphylla) descending to the seafloor. Image by ROV SuBastian/Schmidt Ocean Institute (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0).

Elizabeth Claire Alberts is a senior staff writer for Mongabay and was a 2024-2025 fellow with the Pulitzer Center’s Ocean Reporting Network. Find her on Bluesky and LinkedIn.

Experts say ‘bare bones’ US laws are unfit to regulate nascent deep-sea mining industry

US prepares to auction leases for seabed mining blocks in federal waters

Source: Mongabay | Published: 2026-11-20 22:18 UTC

item.title: Cop31 talks go into overtime as debate rages over lack of fossil fuels in draft deal
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Crucial climate talks headed into overtime on the last official day of the Cop31 UN summit as countries continued to argue over a draft deal that was silent on fossil fuels, with a host of other contentious issues complicating negotiations.

Nearly 200 countries struggled to bridge their differences after two weeks of intense talks and impassioned speeches in Antalya, Turkey, about the effects of climate breakdown around the world, with a scheduled finish of Friday evening breached.

“At this point, no one is happy,” Brazil’s national secretary for climate change, Aloisio Lopes Pereira de Melo, told reporters.

The Guardian understands there will probably not be a new draft of an agreement for negotiators to pore over until Saturday morning. A sprawling initial draft deal released earlier this week included strong calls to accelerate the phase-out of coal, oil and gas, but a second, shorter version on Thursday did not include mention of fossil fuels and weakened goals on electrification.

On Friday there was a dramatic intervention by African ministers early on in the day, with one saying: “We didn’t come here to beg.” Civil society groups, who have a mandated role at the talks, declared it the “worst Cop ever”, with none of their priorities making it through the negotiations. They were particularly frustrated by a failure to take forward a just transition mechanism agreed last year, which they hoped would embed social, racial and economic justice into a low-carbon future.

Several Cop insiders said Saudi Arabia was one of the countries playing an obstructive role. The petrostate has gained a reputation over the decades for using the Cop process to slow action. Saudi Arabia is understood to be among the countries pushing for carbon capture utilisation and storage (CCUS) to be strongly referenced in the final agreement as a way to help the planet to minimise overshooting the 1.5C temperature goal agreed in Paris.

Neil Grant, a senior expert on mitigation at the advisory group Climate Analytics, said CCUS was being put into the text “because the fossil fuel interests want it in there”. He said: “It’s a Trojan horse for fossil fuel interests.”

Eight countries called for reference to “a clear transition away from fossil fuels” to be restored into the text of any agreement. Panama, Belgium, Côte d’Ivoire, Finland, Greece, the Solomon Islands and Sweden outlined vital issues they said must be addressed, including ensuring polluting countries paid into funds for developing countries to adapt to the climate crisis.

Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama’s climate minister, said: “It is not acceptable to have a Cop or a cover document that does not even mention fossil fuels, and we simply will not put up with it. We need to tell the truth and to speak clearly.”

Panama had sent an open letter to the president of the negotiations, Australian climate change minister Chris Bowen, with a list of demands the country said were not negotiable.

“Well, red lines – that’s how negotiations work,” said Bowen. On Friday afternoon, he said: “There is still a spirit of making it work. People have strong views, of course. I’m not stepping away from that. But no one has said to me, let’s give up and go home.”

In a dramatic press conference on Friday morning, African ministers from Ghana, Zambia, Senegal, Kenya and Sierra Leone said African people were being asked to pay for a crisis they did not cause. They accused rich countries of simultaneously attempting a third exploitation of the continent – after slavery and colonialism – by using carbon taxes to prevent Africans from making use of their wealth of critical minerals to industrialise.

Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings of Ghana, who was ministerial chair of the African group of negotiators, said: “The continent will not accept an outcome that offers declarations without the resources to deliver them. We didn’t come here to beg. We came here to claim what is rightfully ours for our people who are suffering the brunt of anthropogenic activities of developed countries, that they are now being asked to pay for in ways that they never asked.”

A vital request of African nations was for discussion of climate finance. All week civil society observers have accused richer countries, led by the EU, of obstructing progress in talks on money.

The chief climate negotiator for Europe said on Friday that it was already the world leading climate finance donor. A senior EU official said: “We, together with the EU member states, are providing €32.3bn [£27bn] from public sources and mobilising €9.3bn in private finance in 2025 to support developing countries. We’re doing by far the most.”

The last Cop meeting to finish on time was in Italy in 2003. Some talks have dragged into the Sunday after the scheduled Friday finish.

Source: The Guardian Environment | Published: 2026-11-20 20:04 UTC

Original link: https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/nov/20/cop31-talks-overtime-fossil-fuels-vanish-from-draft-deal

item.title: Renovated BUGarium in the US aims to connect people and insects
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

For many people a trip to the zoo is an opportunity to see favorite animals like gorillas, giraffes and lions. But in Alburquerque, New Mexico, U.S., visitors can add spiders, scorpions and ants to their must-see list at the ABQ BioPark BUGarium. The facility also includes an aquarium, traditional zoo and botanic garden.

The BUGarium was closed for a year and reopened in October 2026 following a $1.45 million renovation.

Insects are the largest group of animals on Earth, and ecologically essential as pollinators and the base of many food chains. Famed entomologist E.O. Wilson once said: “If we were to wipe out insects alone — just that group alone — on this planet, which we are trying hard to do, the rest of life and humanity with it would mostly disappear from the land. And within a few months.”

The BUGarium exists to educate the public about the importance of insects. “Whether they’re pollinating plants, recycling nutrients, controlling pests, or supporting entire food webs, these animals are essential to healthy ecosystems,” said ABQ BioPark Associate Director Matthew Peterson in a statement.

Bugs are not always an easy sell. “Guests come to the BUGarium with a wide spectrum of attitudes ranging from disgust and horror to fascination and awe,” Alexandra Miller, the curator of entomology at the ABQ BioPark told Mongabay in an email. “We hope guests learn how important arthropods are to ecosystems around the world, what they can do to support native populations, and that arthropods require specialized care in the same way gorillas and elephants do.”

Along with spiders, scorpions, crabs and other animals with jointed exoskeletons insects are part of the taxonomic group Arthropoda.

A highlight of the insect-based zoo is a leaf-cutter ant (Atta cephalotes) colony from a rainforest in Trinidad. It shows the complex society of ants that farm fungus, their food, on leaves that they forage.

“The different chambers the ants live in are made out of blown glass, so guests have the opportunity to see how the entire ant colony operates and works cooperatively,” Miller said.

The BUGarium also exhibits insects and spiders from New Mexico’s Chihuahuan Desert.

“Connecting our guests to nature is a cornerstone of what we do at the BioPark, and at the BUGarium our focus is creating meaningful connections between guests and arthropods,” Miller said.

Other U.S. zoos like the San Diego Zoo and Cincinnati Zoo also have dedicated exhibits for connecting people with insects. However, insect and spider exhibits are not nearly as common as exhibits of popular vertebrate species.

“The BUGarium is part of a small group of facilities dedicated to live insects and arthropods in the United States. Our numbers may be small, but like the animals in our care, can have a huge impact,” Miller said. “We are proud to be a part of the story of connecting people to arthropods and promoting their conservation.”

Banner image: Leaf-cutter ants at ABQ BioPark BUGarium.

Source: Mongabay | Published: 2026-11-20 19:59 UTC

item.title: Trump Administration Awards First-Ever Deep-Sea Mining Exploration Leases
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

In a historic first, the Department of Interior has leased more than 31 million acres of Pacific waters to a deep-sea mining company seeking to exploit mineral-rich deposits from the ocean floor off American Samoa.

“This is the first time that a lease has been issued for deep-sea mining in U.S. waters,” said Arlo Hemphill, U.S. project lead against deep-sea mining for Greenpeace USA.

Deep-sea mining is a highly contested, emerging industry that aims to extract rock-like deposits on the seabed called polymetallic nodules, formed over millions of years. They contain cobalt, copper, manganese and nickel—so-called “critical minerals” used in batteries, electronics and other devices that have historically been mined on land. To date, no commercial deep-sea mining operations have begun anywhere in the world.

Scientists, environmentalists and Indigenous peoples with strong cultural connections to the ocean aim to stop the industry from moving forward at all.

“Once mining strips away habitat that took millions of years to form, no amount of money can bring it back,” said Hemphill in a statement. “Congress should press the administration to suspend these leases before work begins.”

The lease sale took place Thursday, during a live auction held at the Ventura County Fire Department in Thousand Oaks, California, as Hemphill and dozens of other activists from American Samoa and across the Pacific rallied, prayed and sang outside in protest.

“This is not just seabed on a map. This is our home, our livelihoods, our identity, and our responsibility to protect,” said Sabrina Suluai-Mahuka, founder of Finafinau, American Samoa’s youth and environment nonprofit, who traveled from American Samoa to protest the auction. “Ocean rights are human rights, and our home is not for sale,” she said in a statement.

Representatives from just two companies attended the auction, including Adepth Minerals Inc., from Norway, and Wetstone U.S. Ventures, a New York-based offshore critical minerals exploration and deep-sea mining company.

Ultimately, Wetstone bid $6 million on two areas marked for mineral exploration that lie adjacent to the Rose Atoll Marine National Monument, a marine protected area established by President George W. Bush in 2009 to protect more than 10,000 square miles of ocean from commercial fishing and other forms of extraction.

The bid made Wetstone the provisional winner of the auction, according to a spokesperson from the Marine Minerals Administration. The new office was established earlier this year within the Department of Interior to help promote the Trump administration’s agenda to secure critical minerals.

“A dependable critical minerals supply chain is essential to American manufacturing and the technologies that power our economy and national defense,” said Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum, in a statement about Thursday’s auction. “Today’s sale opens a path to learn more about the resources off the coast of American Samoa and assess whether they could contribute to a more reliable domestic supply.”

The areas offered for leasing will be open for exploration activities, which include mapping and surveying the seabed to locate mineral rich deposits. Actual mining would require further federal approvals. But Hemphill and others warn that exploration in itself is a dangerous step towards paving the way for an industry that could threaten ocean ecosystems and the people that depend on them.

“The industry will push to move from surveys to exploration to extraction, putting profits ahead of marine life and trampling the culture, livelihood and objections of communities that have said no again and again,” Hemphill said.

Ever since the proposed lease sale was announced earlier this year, many American Samoan leaders and communities have voiced their concerns. Several lawsuits were filed against the Trump Administration to stop it from happening.

Just a few days before the lease sale, a federal judge in Hawaiʻi ruled the Marine Minerals Administration had violated the Endangered Species Act by approving the lease sale without taking into account the potential impacts of exploration and mining on endangered species.

The areas leased are home to several dozen endangered species including the blue whale, fin whale, sei whale and sperm whale, as well as the leatherback sea turtle, oceanic whitetip shark and giant manta ray.

Many of these species are already threatened by climate change, which is altering their sources of prey and migration patterns. More than 1000 marine science and policy experts from 75 countries say deep-sea mining could further add to the stress these marine animals are facing.

“In deciding to move forward with today’s scheduled sale, the Trump administration has performed a renegade, unlawful act,” said Chris Eaton, attorney at Earthjustice, an environmental nonprofit that represented American Samoan and Hawaiian plaintiffs in the lawsuit. “We will use the full extent of the law to vigorously push for the leases to be voided,” he said in a statement Thursday.
